questions.question: Keeping copies of the same data on several machines immediately introduces which risk?

options.text: The copies can disagree with one another
Reads become slower than on a single machine
Writes can no longer be made durable at all
The schema can no longer be evolved safely

questions.explanation: All of the difficulty in replication lies in handling changes to replicated data: every write must reach every replica, and until it does the replicas hold different values.

questions.question: Define replication.

options.text: Keeping a copy of the same data on several networked machines
Splitting data across multiple machines so each holds a subset
Keeping multiple versions of the same data on one machine
Copying data between a database and a data warehouse

questions.explanation: That second option describes partitioning, which is Chapter 6.

questions.question: Why would you want to replicate data? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: To keep data geographically close to your users, and thus reduce latency
To allow the system to continue working even if some of its parts have failed, and thus increase availability
To scale out the number of machines that can serve read queries, and thus increase read throughput
To store more data than fits on a single machine, and thus increase total storage capacity

questions.explanation: Storing more data than fits on one machine is partitioning, not replication — and this chapter explicitly assumes each machine can hold a copy of the entire dataset.

questions.question: What size assumption does Chapter 5 make, and where is it relaxed?

options.text: That the dataset is small enough for every machine to hold it all
That the dataset exceeds one machine; Chapter 6 relaxes it under replication
That the dataset fits in memory; Chapter 3 relaxes it
That no assumption about dataset size is needed, because replication is independent of volume

questions.explanation: Replication and partitioning are treated as orthogonal concerns, taken one at a time.

questions.question: In which case is replication easy, and why?

options.text: If the replicated data never changes — copy it once and you're done
If there is only one replica, since no coordination is needed
If replication is synchronous, since ordering is guaranteed
If the dataset is small enough to fit in memory

questions.explanation: Static data makes replication a one-off copy; mutation is what makes it an algorithm.

questions.question: Name the three replication algorithms, and how much of the field do they cover?

options.text: Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless — almost all databases use one
Synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous replication; most databases use one of the three
Statement-based, WAL shipping and logical log replication; these cover all databases
Primary-backup, chain and quorum replication; a few databases use others

questions.explanation: Those three are the chapter's organizing structure. Statement-based, WAL shipping and logical logs are implementations of the replication log, a separate axis.

questions.question: Which two trade-offs must be decided, and where are they usually configured?

options.text: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication, and how to handle failed replicas
Which consistency model to use and how many replicas to keep; these are hardcoded
Which topology to use and which conflict resolver to apply; these are chosen by the client
Whether to partition and whether to replicate; these are schema decisions

questions.explanation: Which is why the knowledge transfers between products even though the knobs are named differently.

questions.question: Replication has been studied since the 1970s and the principles haven't changed much. Why not, and why is there still so much misunderstanding?

options.text: Because the fundamental constraints of networks have not changed
Because the algorithms were proven optimal; misunderstanding comes from poor documentation
Because hardware has not improved; misunderstanding comes from vendor marketing
Because the problem is undecidable; misunderstanding is inherent

questions.explanation: Network constraints are the invariant; single-node assumptions are the source of the confusion.

questions.question: Define replica, and state the question that 'inevitably arises' once you have several.

options.text: A replica is any node holding a copy; every write must reach every replica
A replica is a partition of the data; the question is how to route queries
A replica is a backup; the question is how often to take one
A replica is a follower; the question is who becomes leader

questions.explanation: Every write to every replica is the constraint that all three algorithms are answers to.

questions.question: State the three steps of leader-based replication. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One of the replicas is designated the leader; when clients want to write to the database they must send their requests to the leader, which first writes the new data to its local storage

The other replicas are followers; whenever the leader writes new data to its local storage it also sends the data change to all of its followers as part of a replication log or change stream, and each follower applies all writes in the same order as they were processed on the leader
Reads can go to the leader or any follower, but writes are only accepted on the leader — the followers are read-only from the client's point of view
Followers may accept writes directly from clients provided they forward each one to the leader, which then re-broadcasts it to the remaining followers in its own log order

questions.explanation: Same-order application on followers is what keeps the replicas consistent with the leader.

questions.question: Which alternative names exist for leader-based replication and its roles? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The scheme is also known as active/passive replication
The leader is also called the primary
Followers are also called read replicas, secondaries, or hot standbys
The scheme is also known as quorum replication

questions.explanation: A footnote on 'hot standbys' notes that different people have different definitions for hot, warm and cold standbys — in PostgreSQL a hot standby accepts reads from clients while a warm standby doesn't process any queries from clients.

questions.question: Which relational databases have leader-based replication built in? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: PostgreSQL, from version 9.0 onward
MySQL
Oracle Data Guard and SQL Server's AlwaysOn Availability Groups
SQLite, plus Microsoft Access and dBase

questions.explanation: Beyond relational databases it is also used in MongoDB, RethinkDB and Espresso, in message brokers such as Kafka and RabbitMQ highly available queues, and in some network filesystems and replicated block devices such as DRBD — so leader-based replication is not restricted to only databases.

questions.question: Is the choice between synchronous and asynchronous replication configurable?

options.text: Often configurable in relational databases; hardcoded in many others
It is always configurable, in every database that supports replication at all
It is never configurable, being a fixed property of the replication algorithm
It is configurable only in leaderless systems, never in leader-based ones

questions.explanation: A precise, hedged statement — not a universal rule.

questions.question: With a synchronous follower, what does the leader wait for confirmation before doing?

options.text: Before reporting success, and before the write is visible to others
Before reporting success to the user, and before writing to its own local storage
Before making the write visible to other clients, and before compacting the log
Only before reporting success to the user

questions.explanation: Most readers remember only the first. Visibility to other clients is the second, and it is what makes the guarantee meaningful.

questions.question: How fast is replication 'normally', and when could a follower fall behind by several minutes or more? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Most database systems apply changes to followers in less than a second, but there is no guarantee of how long it might take
When a follower is recovering from a failure
When the system is operating near maximum capacity, or when there are network problems between the nodes
When the leader is idle, because followers only poll for changes periodically

questions.explanation: Sub-second in practice, unbounded in principle.

questions.question: State the advantage and disadvantage of synchronous replication.

options.text: The follower is guaranteed current; but a slow follower blocks all writes
Advantage: higher write throughput. Disadvantage: possible data loss on failover
Advantage: lower latency. Disadvantage: followers may diverge
Advantage: no conflicts. Disadvantage: requires a quorum

questions.explanation: Durability guarantee bought with availability of the write path.

questions.question: Why is it impractical for all followers to be synchronous, and what is used in practice?

options.text: Because any single node outage would halt the whole system
Because the leader cannot track more than one follower; in practice all followers are asynchronous
Because network bandwidth is insufficient; in practice a quorum is used
Because followers would conflict; in practice a chain is used

questions.explanation: Under semi-synchronous, at least two nodes are guaranteed to hold an up-to-date copy of the data: the leader and one synchronous follower.

questions.question: State what is lost and gained under fully asynchronous leader-based replication. Be precise about durability.

options.text: Unreplicated writes are lost, so a confirmed write isn't durable
Writes are durable but reads may be stale; the advantage is lower latency
Every acknowledged write survives, and the advantage is simply higher write throughput
Writes are lost only if a follower fails; the advantage is simpler failover

questions.explanation: 'Even if it has been confirmed to the client' is the precise and uncomfortable part.

questions.question: Under which conditions is asynchronous replication nevertheless widely used? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Especially if there are many followers
Especially if the followers are geographically distributed
Especially if the workload is read-only
Especially if durability is the top priority

questions.explanation: Weakening durability may sound like a bad trade-off, but both conditions make synchronous replication prohibitively slow or fragile.

questions.question: What does the boxed aside on replication research name?

options.text: Chain replication, used in systems such as Microsoft Azure Storage
Paxos replication, implemented in Google Spanner, connected to partitioning
Gossip replication, implemented in Cassandra, connected to CRDTs
Quorum replication, implemented in Riak, connected to transactions

questions.explanation: The chapter says it concentrates on the simpler forms of replication that are most commonly used in databases in practice, though data loss in asynchronous systems can be a serious problem.

questions.question: Why is simply copying data files from one node to another not sufficient for setting up a new follower?

options.text: Because clients keep writing, so the file copy would be internally inconsistent
Because the on-disk file formats differ between nodes running different versions
Because copying a large data directory would take far too long to be practical
Because the copied files would carry the wrong ownership and permissions

questions.explanation: The obvious fix — locking the database to make files consistent — is rejected because it would go against the goal of high availability; setting up a follower can usually be done without downtime.

questions.question: List the four steps for setting up a new follower without downtime. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Take a consistent snapshot of the leader's database at some point in time, if possible without taking a lock on the entire database — most databases have this feature as it is also required for backups, for example innobackupex for MySQL
Copy the snapshot to the new follower node

The follower connects to the leader and requests all data changes that have happened since the snapshot was taken, which requires that the snapshot is associated with an exact position in the leader's replication log
Stop accepting writes on the leader until the new follower confirms it has caught up, then reopen the leader to client writes once the two are byte-identical

questions.explanation: Halting writes would defeat the purpose, which is to set up a follower without downtime. The genuine fourth step is that once the follower has processed the backlog since the snapshot, we say it has caught up and it continues processing changes as they happen. PostgreSQL calls the log position the log sequence number; MySQL calls it binlog coordinates. How much of this is automated varies significantly by database — sometimes fully automated, sometimes an arcane multi-step workflow performed manually by an administrator.

questions.question: What is the surprising truth about why nodes go down?

options.text: A node may be down for planned maintenance as readily as for a fault
That most outages are caused by network faults rather than by node faults themselves
That hardware faults dominate every other cause of node unavailability in practice
That software bugs are the most common reason a node stops responding at all

questions.explanation: Which is why the goal is to keep the system as a whole running despite individual node failures, and to keep the impact of a node outage as small as possible.

questions.question: Describe follower failure recovery, and why it is 'quite easy'.

options.text: Catch-up recovery: the follower's own log tells it where to resume
It must be rebuilt from a fresh snapshot of the leader every time it restarts
The leader replays its entire replication log from the very beginning for it
An election is held to choose a new leader, and the old follower is discarded

questions.explanation: The local log gives the follower a known resume point, which is exactly what leader failure lacks.

questions.question: Failover is 'trickier'. What must happen when a leader fails? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader
Clients need to be reconfigured to send their writes to the new leader
The other followers need to start consuming data changes from the new leader
All of the data must be re-replicated from scratch onto every remaining replica

questions.explanation: Those three steps are what the chapter calls failover, which can happen manually or automatically.

questions.question: Step 1 of automatic failover is determining that the leader has failed. What mechanism is used, and what timeout is typical?

options.text: A timeout — say 30 seconds without a response means the node is dead
A heartbeat from a central monitor; the example is 5 seconds
A consensus vote before every write; no number is given
A hardware watchdog; the example is 1 second

questions.explanation: Many things could potentially go wrong — crashes, power outages, network issues — and a timeout cannot distinguish them.

questions.question: Step 2 is choosing a new leader. Which mechanisms are used, and what is this problem called?

options.text: An election by majority, or appointment by an elected controller node
The longest-running replica is always chosen; this is the leader election problem
The replica with the lowest ID is chosen; this is the ordering problem
The client chooses; this is the routing problem

questions.explanation: Most-up-to-date to minimize data loss, agreed by consensus.

questions.question: Step 3 is reconfiguring the system. What is the specific danger when the old leader comes back?

options.text: It may still believe it is the leader and must be made to step down
It will have lost all of its data and must be rebuilt from a leader snapshot
It will automatically overwrite the new leader's log with its own longer one
It will refuse to rejoin the cluster until an administrator intervenes

questions.explanation: Clients also need to send their write requests to the new leader — the chapter cross-references Request Routing.

questions.question: With asynchronous replication, what can go wrong at failover, and what is the most common solution?

options.text: The new leader may lack some of the old leader's writes
The old leader's writes are always merged in; no data is lost
The new leader replays the old leader's log in full
The cluster refuses writes until the old leader returns

questions.explanation: Silently discarding acknowledged writes is the standard, uncomfortable resolution.

questions.question: Trace the GitHub incident the chapter describes.

options.text: An out-of-date MySQL follower was promoted and reused primary keys
A split brain caused two leaders to accept conflicting writes, corrupting the repository index
A network partition caused all writes to be lost for an hour
A failover timeout was set too short, causing repeated unnecessary failovers

questions.explanation: Discarding writes is especially dangerous if other storage systems outside of the database need to be coordinated with the database contents.

questions.question: Define split brain, and name the safety catch and its failure mode.

options.text: Two nodes both believe they are the leader, so writes may be corrupted
Split brain is when a node loses its data; the catch is called fencing and it always works
Split brain is when followers diverge; the catch is called quorum and it can cause data loss
Split brain is when the network partitions; the catch is called STONITH and it prevents all writes

questions.explanation: The catch can overshoot and kill both nodes — fencing is discussed in more detail in Chapter 8.

questions.question: State both directions of the timeout trade-off for declaring a leader dead.

options.text: Long timeouts delay recovery; short ones cause unnecessary failovers
Longer timeouts cause unnecessary failovers; shorter timeouts delay recovery
The timeout has no effect on recovery time
Timeouts should always be as short as possible

questions.explanation: Unnecessary failover under load is a positive feedback loop, which is why manual failover survives.

questions.question: Which fundamental problems of distributed systems does failover expose?

options.text: Node failures, unreliable networks, and consistency trade-offs
Clock skew, garbage collection pauses and disk failures — discussed in Chapter 3
Conflict resolution, topology and quorum size — discussed in Chapter 6
Schema evolution, encoding and compatibility — discussed in Chapter 4

questions.explanation: The failover discussion is a preview of the distributed-systems chapters.

questions.question: Describe statement-based replication.

options.text: The leader logs and ships every write statement for followers to execute
The leader sends its write-ahead log to followers, which apply it byte for byte
The leader sends row-level change records to followers
Followers poll the leader for changed rows

questions.explanation: Sending the statement rather than its effect is what makes determinism a requirement.

questions.question: Which ways can statement-based replication break down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Nondeterministic functions — any statement calling NOW() to get the current date and time or RAND() to get a random number is likely to generate a different value on each replica

Order dependence — if statements use an autoincrementing column or depend on the existing data (such as UPDATE ... WHERE some condition), they must be executed in exactly the same order on each replica, which can be limiting when there are multiple concurrently executing transactions

Side effects — statements that have side effects such as triggers, stored procedures and user-defined functions may result in different side effects occurring on each replica, unless the side effects are absolutely deterministic
Encoding differences — a statement written against one character set cannot be parsed by a replica configured with another, so the follower skips the write and logs a warning to its error log instead

questions.explanation: Three ways, all reducible to nondeterminism.

questions.question: What is the workaround for nondeterminism, why is it not enough, and who still uses statement-based replication?

options.text: Replace nondeterministic calls with a fixed value when logging
Followers ask the leader for function values; MySQL still uses it exclusively
Nondeterministic function calls are rejected at parse time, and VoltDB alone still ships statement-based replication
The edge cases are unsolvable, which is why every database has abandoned statement-based replication entirely

questions.explanation: VoltDB pushes the determinism requirement up to the application, which makes the approach safe.

questions.question: What makes WAL shipping possible across both storage-engine families?

options.text: Both engines keep an append-only byte log of every write
Both engines store table rows on disk in exactly the same physical format
Both engines already expose a logical, row-level change stream to clients
Both engines organize their storage into pages of one fixed size

questions.explanation: Byte-level identity of the log is what lets the follower reconstruct byte-level identical structures — and also what couples it to the engine.

questions.question: Which databases use WAL shipping, and what is its main disadvantage?

options.text: PostgreSQL and Oracle; the log is tied to the storage engine internals
MySQL and MongoDB; the disadvantage is that the log is too large
Cassandra and Riak; the disadvantage is nondeterminism
PostgreSQL and MySQL; the disadvantage is that triggers are not replicated

questions.explanation: Storage-format coupling is the cost of byte-level fidelity.

questions.question: What is the operational impact of WAL shipping's version coupling?

options.text: Followers can be upgraded first, enabling a zero-downtime upgrade
Upgrades are faster but riskier
Upgrades require rebuilding all followers from snapshots
Version coupling has no operational consequence, since a failover always restarts every node on the same build

questions.explanation: What looks like a minor implementation detail costs you the zero-downtime upgrade path.

questions.question: Define a logical log, and state what a row-level record must contain in each case. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A logical log uses different log formats for replication and for the storage engine, which allows the replication log to be decoupled from the storage engine internals — 'logical' as distinct from the storage engine's physical data representation. It is usually a sequence of records describing writes to database tables at the granularity of a row
For an inserted row, the log contains the new values of all columns
For a deleted row, the log contains enough information to uniquely identify the row that was deleted — typically the primary key, or if there is no primary key, the old values of all columns
For an updated row, the log holds only the primary key, and each follower re-reads the changed column values from the leader on demand before applying

questions.explanation: A follower never reads back from the leader. For an updated row the log contains enough information to identify the row plus the new values of all columns that changed. A transaction that modifies several rows generates several such log records, followed by a record indicating that the transaction was committed. MySQL's binlog, when configured to use row-based replication, uses this approach.

questions.question: Which benefits does decoupling the replication log from the storage engine give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can more easily be kept backward compatible, allowing the leader and followers to run different versions of the database software, or even different storage engines

A logical log format is easier for external applications to parse — useful for sending database contents to an external system such as a data warehouse for offline analysis, or for building custom indexes and caches
This technique is called change data capture, returned to in Chapter 11
It shrinks the replication log by roughly a factor of ten, because column names are replaced by numeric field tags

questions.explanation: Version independence enables rolling upgrades; parseability enables change data capture.

questions.question: In which circumstances might you need trigger-based replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you want to only replicate a subset of the data
If you want to replicate from one kind of database to another
If you need conflict resolution logic
If you need lower latency than the database's built-in replication

questions.explanation: All three require replication functionality the database doesn't provide, so it has to move up to the application layer.

questions.question: How does trigger-based replication work, and which products use it?

options.text: Custom application code that fires on a write and logs it to a table
Triggers push changes directly to remote replicas over the network with no intermediate table
Triggers rewrite the WAL; the products are PostgreSQL and MySQL
Triggers are not usable for replication at all

questions.explanation: The separate table is the handoff point between the database and the external replication process.

questions.question: What is the verdict on trigger-based replication?

options.text: Greater overhead and more bugs than built-in replication, but flexible
It is the preferred replication method for most production deployments today
It carries no measurable overhead, but it is completely inflexible in use
It is faster than WAL shipping, at the cost of weaker durability guarantees

questions.explanation: Two costs and one redeeming property.

questions.question: Describe the read-scaling architecture and its benefits.

options.text: Writes go only to the leader, but reads can spread across many followers
Writes are distributed across replicas, increasing write throughput
Reads go only to the leader, which is cached
Both reads and writes scale linearly with the number of nodes

questions.explanation: Reads scale; writes do not. That asymmetry is inherent to single-leader replication.

questions.question: Why does the read-scaling architecture only realistically work with asynchronous replication?

options.text: Because one node failure would then make the whole system unwritable
Because synchronous replication cannot serve read queries from its followers
Because asynchronous replication is always faster, whatever the node count
Because followers have no mechanism for acknowledging a write to the leader

questions.explanation: The probability of at least one node being down grows with node count, so synchronous fan-out and read scaling are in direct conflict.

questions.question: Define eventual consistency, and what does the definition deliberately leave out?

options.text: Reads from a lagging follower may be stale, but only temporarily
All replicas are always consistent within one second
Replicas converge regardless of whether writes continue
Reads always return the most recent write

questions.explanation: The catch-up is only promised in the absence of further writes — which is what makes the guarantee so weak in a live system.

questions.question: Where does the term 'eventual consistency' come from, and does it apply only to NoSQL?

options.text: Coined by Douglas Terry et al. and popularized by Werner Vogels
The term was coined by Werner Vogels and applies only to NoSQL databases
The term was coined by Leslie Lamport and applies only to consensus systems
The term has no traceable origin

questions.explanation: The correction matters: eventual consistency is a property of asynchronous replication, not of a product category.

questions.question: How large is replication lag in practice, and what is its upper bound?

options.text: Often a fraction of a second, but there is no upper bound at all
Always under one second, bounded by the replication timeout
Bounded by the configured maximum lag setting
Bounded at 30 seconds by the failover timeout

questions.explanation: Replication lag is the delay between a write happening on the leader and being reflected on a follower. 'Eventually' is deliberately vague.

questions.question: Name the three replication-lag anomalies this section covers, and the guarantee that fixes each.

options.text: Read-after-write, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix reads
Stale reads, fixed by quorums; lost writes, fixed by fencing; conflicts, fixed by CRDTs
Split brain, fixed by STONITH; data loss, fixed by synchronous replication; lag, fixed by monitoring
Dirty reads, phantom reads and write skew, fixed by transaction isolation

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses these inconsistencies are not just a theoretical issue but a real problem for applications.

questions.question: Describe the setup that produces the read-your-writes anomaly.

options.text: The user's own write may not have reached the follower they read from
It happens only when the write itself was sent to a follower rather than the leader
It happens only under synchronous replication, where the leader waits for followers
It happens only when the read crosses a datacenter boundary to a remote replica

questions.explanation: The user's own write appearing to vanish is the most user-visible replication-lag symptom.

questions.question: State exactly what read-after-write consistency guarantees — and what it does not.

options.text: The user always sees their own updates, with no promise about others'
It guarantees all users see all writes immediately
It guarantees the user sees other users' writes but not necessarily their own
It guarantees strong consistency across all replicas

questions.explanation: A per-user guarantee, not a global one.

questions.question: Describe the first implementation technique for read-after-write consistency, and its awkward precondition.

options.text: Read from the leader anything the user may have modified
Always read from the leader, which requires no precondition
Read from the follower with the lowest lag, which requires lag monitoring
Read twice and compare, which requires idempotent reads

questions.explanation: The precondition is knowing what might be modified before you ask, which is what makes this technique brittle.

questions.question: When most things are user-editable, what are the two separate uses of 'one minute' in the alternative technique?

options.text: Read from the leader for a minute after any update, and watch lag
Both of them refer to the failover timeout that decides when a leader is dead
One refers to cache expiry and the other to the length of the user's session
Both refer to how long the leader retains its replication log before truncating

questions.explanation: One is a per-user read window; the other is a per-follower eligibility threshold. Otherwise most things would have to be read from the leader, negating the benefit of read scaling.

questions.question: Describe the timestamp-remembering technique and its clock caveat.

options.text: The client remembers its last write timestamp and requires that freshness
The server remembers each client's last write; no clocks are involved
The client polls until the data appears; no timestamps are needed
The leader stamps every read with its own clock, making skew between the replicas irrelevant to the guarantee

questions.explanation: Logical timestamps avoid the clock problem; wall-clock timestamps reintroduce it.

questions.question: What complexity do multiple datacenters add to read-after-write consistency?

options.text: Leader-bound requests must be routed to the leader's own datacenter
Routing is unaffected, because each datacenter keeps its own independent leader
Timestamps become meaningless across datacenters
Reads must be served from all datacenters simultaneously

questions.explanation: Leader-directed reads turn into cross-datacenter routing decisions.

questions.question: Define cross-device read-after-write consistency and its additional issues. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the user enters some information on one device — say a desktop web browser — and then views it on another device such as a mobile app, they should see the information they just entered

Approaches that require remembering the timestamp of the user's last update become more difficult, because the code running on one device doesn't know what updates have happened on the other device; this metadata needs to be centralized

If replicas are distributed across different datacenters there is no guarantee that connections from different devices will be routed to the same datacenter — for example if the user's computer uses the home broadband connection and their mobile device uses the cellular data network, the devices' network routes may be completely different. So if your approach requires reading from the leader, you may first need to route requests from all of a user's devices to the same datacenter
Devices cannot share one user identity across platforms, which makes cross-device read-after-write impossible to provide at all, so the guarantee is abandoned in favour of per-device consistency

questions.explanation: Two issues: centralizing the metadata, and routing devices consistently.

questions.question: A user queries twice and the second query, hitting a more lagged follower, returns less than the first. Trace the anomaly.

options.text: The same query hits a lagging follower second, so time appears to go backward
User 1234 reads the same key twice and sees an identical value on both occasions
User 2345 writes the same key twice and the second of the two writes is lost
User 1234 reads from the leader itself and nonetheless receives a stale value

questions.explanation: Two reads landing on differently-lagged followers is what makes time run backward for the reader.

questions.question: Which of the two outcomes in that anomaly is actually the confusing one?

options.text: That seeing nothing first would have been fine; the disappearance is what confuses
That missing the comment entirely would have been worse than watching it vanish
That both outcomes are equally confusing, so neither is worth designing around
That neither outcome matters to users, who expect some lag in a distributed system

questions.explanation: Ignorance is tolerable; retraction is not.

questions.question: Where does monotonic reads sit in the hierarchy, and what exactly does it rule out?

options.text: Weaker than strong consistency, stronger than eventual consistency
It is stronger than strong consistency and rules out all stale reads
It is equivalent to eventual consistency and rules out nothing
It guarantees reads always return the latest write

questions.explanation: Staleness is permitted; non-monotonicity is not.

questions.question: How is monotonic reads implemented, and what is the operational problem?

options.text: Always read from the same replica, chosen by a hash of the user ID
Always read from the leader; the problem is leader load
Read from all replicas and take the newest; the problem is latency
Use version vectors; the problem is storage overhead

questions.explanation: Sticky routing by user hash, with failover as the weak point.

questions.question: In the consistent-prefix-reads dialog, what is the causal dependency and what does a third listener hear?

options.text: The answer is causally dependent on the question, so order matters
The two lines are causally independent, so any order an observer sees is equally valid
Mr. Poons's question depends on Mrs. Cake's answer; the observer hears nothing
The dialog illustrates monotonic reads, not consistent prefix reads

questions.explanation: Figure 5-5's caption: if some partitions are replicated slower than others, an observer may see the answer before they see the question.

questions.question: State the consistent prefix reads guarantee, and where it is a particular problem.

options.text: Writes seen in one order are seen in that order by every reader
All reads return the newest write; it is a problem only in single-node databases
Reads are monotonic per user; it is a problem only across datacenters
Writes are ordered by timestamp; it is a problem only with clock skew

questions.explanation: Independent partitions without global write ordering is the structural cause.

questions.question: What two approaches give you consistent prefix reads?

options.text: Write causally related data to the same partition
Use a global timestamp on every write, or route all reads to the leader
Use synchronous replication, or disable partitioning
Use quorum reads, or version vectors only

questions.explanation: Co-partition the causally related writes, or track causality explicitly.

questions.question: What thought experiment does 'Solutions for Replication Lag' open with?

options.text: Ask how the application behaves if lag grows to minutes or hours
Measure the average lag and set an SLA at the p99
Assume replication is synchronous and handle exceptions
Disable asynchronous replication in production

questions.explanation: The last sentence is the chapter's warning against wishful design.

questions.question: In one sentence, why do transactions exist?

options.text: That databases should just do the right thing — which is why transactions exist
That transactions exist mainly to improve write throughput on the leader node
That transactions exist mainly to make partitioning transparent to applications
That transactions exist mainly to compress the replication log between nodes

questions.explanation: Framed against the cost of handling these issues in application code, which is complex and easy to get wrong.

questions.question: Many distributed databases abandoned transactions, claiming they are too expensive and eventual consistency is inevitable. How should that claim be judged?

options.text: Some truth, but overly simplistic; a fuller view comes in Chapters 7 and 9
The statement is entirely correct, so transactions should be avoided in distributed systems
The statement is entirely wrong, because transactions are cheap at any scale
The chapter declines to take any position on the cost of transactions at all

questions.explanation: Note both halves: partial truth, overly simplistic.

questions.question: State leader-based replication's 'one major downside'.

options.text: There is only one leader, so losing contact with it means losing writes
Reads cannot be scaled out, because every read must also go to the leader
Conflicts must be resolved by the application, since two leaders may diverge
Followers cannot be added without taking the whole cluster down for a rebuild

questions.explanation: A footnote qualifies it: if the database is partitioned, each partition has one leader, and different partitions may have their leaders on different nodes — but each partition must nevertheless have one leader node.

questions.question: Define the multi-leader configuration, its alternative name, and the dual role each node plays.

options.text: More than one node accepts writes, each acting as follower to the others
It allows any node to accept reads but only one to accept writes; it is called read scaling
It elects a new leader per write; it is called rotating leadership
It has no leaders at all; it is called leaderless replication

questions.explanation: Every node is both leader and follower, which is what creates the conflict problem.

questions.question: Does multi-leader replication make sense within a single datacenter?

options.text: It rarely makes sense within one datacenter, as complexity outweighs benefit
It is the recommended default configuration within a single datacenter
It is required in order to achieve high availability inside one datacenter
It cannot be configured within one datacenter, only between separate ones

questions.explanation: Multi-leader earns its complexity only when there is a real reason for multiple write-accepting locations.

questions.question: Describe the multi-datacenter multi-leader architecture precisely.

options.text: One leader per datacenter, replicating leader-to-leader between them
One global leader replicates to followers in all datacenters
All nodes in all datacenters are leaders with no followers
Each datacenter has followers only, with the leader outside

questions.explanation: Two levels: leader-follower inside, leader-leader across — so you can tolerate the failure of an entire datacenter, or be closer to your users.

questions.question: How do single-leader and multi-leader replication compare across the three dimensions that matter? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Performance — with single-leader, every write must go over the internet to the datacenter with the leader, adding significant latency and arguably contravening the purpose of having multiple datacenters; with multi-leader, every write can be processed in the local datacenter and replicated asynchronously, so the inter-datacenter network delay is hidden from users and perceived performance may be better

Tolerance of datacenter outages — with single-leader, if the datacenter with the leader fails, failover can promote a follower in another datacenter; with multi-leader, each datacenter can continue operating independently of the others, and replication catches up when the failed datacenter comes back online

Tolerance of network problems — traffic between datacenters usually goes over the public internet, which may be less reliable than a local network; a single-leader configuration is very sensitive to problems in this inter-datacenter link because writes are made synchronously over it, whereas a multi-leader configuration with asynchronous replication can usually tolerate network problems better, since a temporary network interruption does not prevent writes being processed
Conflict resolution — a single-leader setup needs it because followers diverge under lag, whereas a multi-leader setup avoids conflicts by construction, since each leader owns a disjoint key range

questions.explanation: The last one is inverted: multi-leader is precisely the configuration that requires conflict resolution.

questions.question: Which external tools retrofit multi-leader replication onto a database? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Tungsten Replicator for MySQL
BDR for PostgreSQL
GoldenGate for Oracle
Bucardo for Cassandra

questions.explanation: Multi-leader is sometimes built in and often bolted on by external tooling.

questions.question: What is the danger in multi-leader replication being 'somewhat retrofitted' onto databases?

options.text: Autoincrementing keys, triggers and constraints all become problematic
That it is slower than single-leader replication in essentially all workloads
That it cannot be used across datacenters, only between nodes in one room
That it requires fully synchronous replication between all of the leaders

questions.explanation: The big problem is that the same data may be concurrently modified in two different datacenters, and those write conflicts must be resolved.

questions.question: Describe the offline-operation use case for multi-leader replication.

options.text: An app that must keep working while disconnected, like a calendar
A read-only local cache that synchronizes whenever connectivity returns
A single-leader setup in which each device runs a local read-only follower
A leaderless store in which each device performs quorum writes when online

questions.explanation: Each device being a leader is what makes offline writes possible.

questions.question: How does offline operation relate to multi-datacenter replication?

options.text: The same as cross-datacenter multi-leader, with each device a datacenter
The two are unrelated architectures that merely happen to share some vocabulary
Offline operation is really a form of leaderless replication with quorum reads
Offline operation is single-leader replication with a very long failover timeout

questions.explanation: The broken-calendar-sync remark is the chapter's dry evidence that this is hard.

questions.question: In real-time collaborative editing, what is the local replica?

options.text: Etherpad and Google Docs, where edits apply locally then replicate
The server holds the only replica; clients are stateless views
Each keystroke is written synchronously to the server
The local replica is a read-only cache

questions.explanation: The browser holding a writable replica is what makes this multi-leader replication.

questions.question: If you want to guarantee there will be no editing conflicts, what must the application do, and what is that equivalent to?

options.text: Lock the document, so the second user waits for the first to release
It must use CRDTs, which is equivalent to leaderless replication
It must version every keystroke, which is equivalent to multi-leader replication
It must resolve conflicts on read, which is equivalent to quorum replication

questions.explanation: Locking eliminates concurrency, which is what single-leader replication does structurally.

questions.question: For faster collaboration you change two things. What are they, and what does that cost?

options.text: Make the unit of change tiny, such as one keystroke, and avoid locking
Increase the unit of change and add locking; the cost is latency
Use synchronous replication and a single leader; the cost is availability
Compress changes and batch them; the cost is bandwidth

questions.explanation: Fine-grained lock-free edits buy responsiveness and inherit every multi-leader problem.

questions.question: Two users concurrently change a wiki page title from A to B and from A to C on different leaders. Trace the conflict.

options.text: Two users set the title differently at the same time on different leaders
Each user's write goes through the same leader, so the second of the two is rejected outright
User 1's write is lost before reaching any leader
The conflict is detected synchronously at write time

questions.explanation: The figure's caption: a write conflict caused by two leaders concurrently updating the same record.

questions.question: Contrast single-leader and multi-leader conflict detection, and explain why making detection synchronous is self-defeating.

options.text: Single-leader blocks or aborts the second write; multi-leader detects late
Both detect conflicts synchronously; the difference is only in resolution
Multi-leader detects conflicts synchronously and single-leader asynchronously
Conflicts go undetected in both setups, leaving the application to discover them when it next reads

questions.explanation: Synchronous detection collapses multi-leader into single-leader.

questions.question: Describe the conflict-avoidance strategy and the 'home' datacenter arrangement.

options.text: Avoid them: route all writes for a record through the same leader
Conflicts are avoided by locking every record before writing
Conflicts are avoided by using synchronous replication
Conflicts cannot be avoided in a multi-leader setup

questions.explanation: Per-user single-leader behaviour inside a multi-leader deployment.

questions.question: Why might conflict avoidance break down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because one datacenter has failed and you need to reroute traffic to another datacenter
Because a user has moved to a different location and is now closer to a different datacenter
Because the record's schema changed between the two writes being applied
Because the replication topology had been reconfigured to all-to-all beforehand

questions.explanation: In either situation conflict avoidance breaks down, and you have to deal with the possibility of concurrent writes on different leaders.

questions.question: If those two writes were simply applied in arrival order at each leader, what value would each hold, and why is neither ordering correct?

options.text: Each leader ends on a different value, leaving a permanent divergence
Both leaders converge on B, so the divergence resolves itself without help
Leader 1 ends at B and leader 2 at C; the earlier write is correct
Both end at C, which is correct because it was written second

questions.explanation: Contrast single-leader, where writes are in a sequential order and the last write determines the final value.

questions.question: Which routes lead to convergent conflict resolution? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Highest ID wins — give each write a unique ID such as a timestamp, long random number, UUID, or hash of the key and value, pick the write with the highest ID as the winner and throw away the other writes. If a timestamp is used, this is known as last write wins (LWW); although popular, it is dangerously prone to data loss
Highest replica number wins — give each replica a unique ID and let writes that originated at a higher-numbered replica always take precedence; this approach also implies data loss
Merge the values together — for example order them alphabetically and then concatenate them, so the merged title might be 'B/C'
Roll both writes back and return an error to each client, so that both users retry against whichever leader wins the election

questions.explanation: Rolling back is single-leader behaviour, not a convergent multi-leader resolution. The fourth genuine route is to record the conflict in an explicit data structure preserving all information, and write application code that resolves it later, perhaps by prompting the user. Four routes, two of which the chapter explicitly flags as data-losing. LWW is discussed in detail at the end of the chapter.

questions.question: Custom conflict resolution code can execute at two moments. Describe both.

options.text: On write, a handler runs in the background; on read, all versions are returned
On commit and on rollback, with the database handling both cases internally
On replication and on compaction, with the storage engine handling both cases
Only on write; a read never surfaces a conflict to the application at all

questions.explanation: The on-write constraint — background process, must be fast, cannot prompt — is what makes on-read resolution attractive.

questions.question: At what granularity does conflict resolution usually apply?

options.text: At the level of an individual row or document, not a whole transaction
At the level of an entire transaction, which is resolved atomically
At the level of an entire table, which is resolved as a single unit
At the level of the whole database, which is resolved at failover time

questions.explanation: Transaction atomicity does not extend to conflict resolution.

questions.question: Recount the Amazon shopping cart conflict-resolution anecdote.

options.text: Amazon's shopping cart kept added items but lost removals
Amazon lost entire carts during a datacenter failover
Amazon's handler merged carts across different customers
Amazon's handler always picked the newest cart, discarding older items

questions.explanation: An asymmetric merge — union of additions, ignoring removals — which is exactly the problem tombstones solve.

questions.question: Name the three lines of automatic conflict-resolution research. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) — a family of data structures for sets, maps, ordered lists, counters and so on that can be concurrently edited by multiple users and automatically resolve conflicts in sensible ways; some have been implemented in Riak 2.0
Mergeable persistent data structures — which track history explicitly, similarly to the Git version control system, and use a three-way merge function, whereas CRDTs use two-way merges

Operational transformation — the conflict resolution algorithm behind collaborative editing applications such as Etherpad and Google Docs, designed particularly for concurrent editing of an ordered list of items, such as the list of characters that constitute a text document
Byzantine fault-tolerant merging — the approach taken by blockchain databases, where individual replicas cannot be trusted to report their own state honestly

questions.explanation: Implementations of these are still young, but it is likely that they will be integrated into more replicated data systems in the future, making multi-leader data synchronization much simpler for applications to deal with.

questions.question: The chapter asks 'What is a conflict?' and gives a subtle example. Why doesn't an availability check save you?

options.text: Two overlapping bookings for one room, each passing its own leader's check
The availability check saves you entirely, so no conflict is possible at all
The check fails because the clocks on the two leaders are not synchronized
The check is unnecessary, because rooms are partitioned across the leaders

questions.explanation: The chapter is honest that there isn't a quick ready-made answer, pointing forward to Chapter 7 and Chapter 12.

questions.question: Define replication topology, and state how many plausible topologies exist with exactly two leaders.

options.text: The communication paths along which writes propagate between nodes
It describes the physical network wiring; with two leaders there are two topologies
It describes the partition assignment; with two leaders there are four topologies
It describes the conflict resolution order; topology count is unbounded

questions.explanation: Two leaders forces the trivial bidirectional case; complexity begins at three.

questions.question: Name the three multi-leader replication topologies, and identify the most general one and MySQL's default.

options.text: Circular, star and all-to-all, the last being the most general
Chain, mesh and tree; chain is the most general and MySQL's default
Circular, star and all-to-all; star is the most general and MySQL's default
Primary-backup, quorum and gossip; gossip is most general

questions.explanation: A footnote warns not to confuse the star topology with a star schema — the former describes the communication topology between nodes, the latter the structure of a data model.

questions.question: In circular and star topologies, what prevents infinite replication loops?

options.text: Each write is tagged with every node identifier it has passed through
A time-to-live counter attached to every write, decremented at each hop
A global sequence number assigned to each write by the root node of the topology
A lock held on the record for as long as the write circulates around the ring

questions.explanation: Writes may need to pass through several nodes before they reach all replicas, so nodes must forward changes they receive from other nodes — hence the need for loop detection.

questions.question: Compare circular and star topologies with all-to-all on fault tolerance.

options.text: One node failure interrupts the whole chain in circular and star topologies
All-to-all is the worst, because it has the largest number of links to fail
All three topologies tolerate a single node failure equally well in practice
Star is the most fault tolerant, because the root node can itself be replicated

questions.explanation: Path redundancy is what density buys.

questions.question: Client A inserts a row on leader 1 and client B updates it on leader 3. What can go wrong at leader 2, and what is the general problem called?

options.text: An update may arrive at a third leader before the insert it depends on
Client A and client B both insert the same row, which causes a duplicate key error
Leader 2 crashes before either write reaches it, so both of the writes are lost
The two writes conflict directly and have to be merged by the application

questions.explanation: Figure 5-9's caption: with multi-leader replication, writes may arrive in the wrong order at some replicas.

questions.question: Why don't timestamps fix that ordering problem, and what technique works instead?

options.text: Timestamps aren't enough because clocks can't be trusted; use version vectors
Timestamps do solve it, provided every node runs NTP against the same source
Timestamps fail only because they are too coarse; sequence numbers solve it
The anomaly cannot be fixed by any technique, so it must simply be tolerated

questions.explanation: Clock skew is why causality needs logical, not physical, ordering — the topic of Detecting Concurrent Writes.

questions.question: Which two real multi-leader systems fall short, and what does each fail to do?

options.text: PostgreSQL BDR lacks causal ordering; Tungsten doesn't detect conflicts
GoldenGate silently loses writes while BDR duplicates them on every leader
Both of them fail to support circular replication topologies at all
Both of them fail to support deployment across more than one datacenter

questions.explanation: Conflict detection techniques are poorly implemented in many multi-leader replication systems.

questions.question: What should you do if you use a multi-leader system? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Be aware of these issues
Carefully read the documentation
Thoroughly test your database to ensure that it really does provide the guarantees you believe it to have
Disable conflict resolution and handle it in the application

questions.explanation: Verify rather than assume — the documentation and the implementation may both overpromise.

questions.question: What do single-leader and multi-leader replication have in common, and what does leaderless replication abandon?

options.text: Both route writes through a leader that fixes the order for followers
Each uses quorums to order writes, whereas leaderless replication abandons quorums
Each is fully synchronous, whereas leaderless replication is always asynchronous
Each relies on conflict resolution, whereas leaderless replication avoids conflicts

questions.explanation: Two properties abandoned: the leader itself, and the leader-imposed write ordering.

questions.question: Trace the history of leaderless replication.

options.text: Early systems were leaderless; Amazon's Dynamo made it fashionable again
It was invented outright by Amazon in 2007 and had no earlier predecessors
It originated with Cassandra and was only later adopted by Amazon for Dynamo
It has always been the dominant architecture, even during the relational era

questions.explanation: A footnote makes a commonly misremembered correction: Dynamo is not available to users outside of Amazon, and AWS offers a hosted database product called DynamoDB which uses a completely different architecture — it is based on single-leader replication.

questions.question: Which open source datastores have leaderless replication models inspired by Dynamo? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Riak
Cassandra
Voldemort
MongoDB

questions.explanation: Hence the label Dynamo-style. MongoDB uses leader-based replication.

questions.question: Who sends writes to the replicas in a leaderless system, and what is the crucial difference from a leader?

options.text: Sometimes the client writes to several replicas, sometimes a coordinator does
A coordinator node that behaves exactly like a leader, enforcing a write order
The replicas gossip among themselves, and clients never write to them directly
A leader elected at random for the duration of each individual write request

questions.explanation: A coordinator without ordering authority is not a leader, which is what keeps the system leaderless.

questions.question: Three replicas, one of them down. Trace a quorum write.

options.text: The client writes to all three; two acknowledge and the third simply misses it
The write fails outright, because one of the three replicas is unavailable
The client blocks until all three replicas have acknowledged the write
A failover promotes a new leader first, after which the write proceeds normally

questions.explanation: Figure 5-10's caption: a quorum write, quorum read, and read repair after a node outage.

questions.question: When the unavailable node returns, what is the problem and the solution on the read path?

options.text: Reads go to several nodes in parallel, and version numbers pick the newest
The returning node is wiped and rebuilt from a snapshot of a healthy replica
The returning node is permanently excluded from serving any read requests
The client reads only from whichever node reports the longest current uptime

questions.explanation: Parallel reads plus version numbers is how staleness is detected without a leader.

questions.question: Describe read repair using version numbers, and say what it works well for.

options.text: The client spots the stale version among the parallel responses and writes back
The client discards the stale value and does nothing further; it works for rarely-read values
The server detects staleness and repairs it in the background; it works for all values equally
The stale replica is removed from the cluster; it works for write-heavy values

questions.explanation: Read repair only fixes what gets read — which is why an anti-entropy process is also needed.

questions.question: Describe the anti-entropy process and what its absence costs.

options.text: A background anti-entropy process that copies missing data between replicas
It copies writes strictly in order like a replication log, and every system has one
It is simply read repair performed at write time rather than at read time
It reduces durability, because it deletes any value that has not been read

questions.explanation: Two differences from a replication log: no ordering, and unbounded delay.

questions.question: Derive the quorum intuition from the three-replica example.

options.text: At most one replica can be stale, so reading two guarantees a fresh value
Writing to one replica and reading from one replica is already sufficient
You must write to all three replicas and also read from all three of them
Reading from a single replica suffices, provided writes always go to all three

questions.explanation: Overlap between the write set and the read set is the whole mechanism.

questions.question: State the general quorum condition with n, w and r, and explain why it works.

options.text: With n replicas, w confirmations per write and r per read, w plus r exceeds n
As long as w plus r is less than n, reads see the latest value
As long as w equals r, reads see the latest value regardless of n
As long as w is greater than r, reads see the latest value

questions.explanation: The chapter's example values are n = 3, w = 2, r = 2. A footnote notes this kind of quorum is sometimes called a strict quorum, to contrast with sloppy quorums.

questions.question: What is the common choice of n, w and r in Dynamo-style databases, and what are the values for n = 3 and n = 5?

options.text: Make n odd and set w and r each to (n + 1) / 2, rounded up
Make n even and set w and r each to n / 2, giving two apiece when n is four
Always set w equal to n and r equal to 1, whatever the number of replicas
Always set w equal to 1 and r equal to n, whatever the number of replicas

questions.explanation: Odd n with a simple majority is the standard configuration. A boxed note adds that you may have more than n nodes in the cluster, with any given value stored only on n nodes, which allows the dataset to be partitioned — supporting datasets larger than you can fit on one node.

questions.question: For a workload with few writes and many reads, which quorum setting fits, and what is its disadvantage?

options.text: Set w = n and r = 1 for fast reads, at the cost of fragile writes
Setting w = 1 and r = n, which makes writes faster with no disadvantage
Setting w = r = 1, which maximizes availability with no staleness
Setting w = r = n, which guarantees consistency at no cost

questions.explanation: It satisfies the quorum condition (n plus 1 is greater than n) but concentrates all the fragility on the write path.

questions.question: Which statements about the quorum condition's tolerance are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If w is less than n, we can still process writes if a node is unavailable; if r is less than n, we can still process reads if a node is unavailable
With n = 3, w = 2, r = 2 we can tolerate one unavailable node; with n = 5, w = 3, r = 3 we can tolerate two unavailable nodes

Normally reads and writes are always sent to all n replicas in parallel — w and r determine how many nodes we wait for, that is, how many of the n nodes need to report success before we consider the read or write to be successful
Reads and writes are sent only to w or to r nodes respectively, chosen at random from the n home nodes responsible for that particular key

questions.explanation: The last one is the mistake readers most often make: w and r are waiting thresholds, not sending counts.

questions.question: If fewer than w or r nodes are available, what happens — and does the reason for unavailability matter?

options.text: The operation simply returns an error, whatever the underlying cause
The operation blocks until enough nodes return; the reason determines the retry policy
The operation succeeds with a warning; only crashes count as unavailable
The coordinator substitutes another node automatically; the reason is logged

questions.explanation: Deliberate indifference to fault type is what keeps the quorum model simple.

questions.question: Why are r and w often chosen to be a majority, and must a quorum always be a majority?

options.text: A majority keeps w plus r above n while tolerating n/2 failures
Because majorities are required by the quorum theorem; no other assignment is valid
Because majorities minimize latency; other assignments are always worse
Because majorities guarantee strong consistency in all cases

questions.explanation: Overlap, not majority, is the actual requirement.

questions.question: What happens if you deliberately set w plus r to be less than or equal to n?

options.text: Fewer successful responses are needed, so stale reads become likelier
The database rejects the configuration outright as an invalid quorum setting
Reads remain guaranteed fresh, but acknowledged writes may silently be lost
Latency increases and availability decreases, which is why it is discouraged

questions.explanation: A deliberate trade of freshness for latency and availability.

questions.question: Even with w plus r greater than n, stale values can be returned. In which scenarios? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sloppy quorum — the w writes may end up on different nodes than the r reads, so there is no longer a guaranteed overlap between the r nodes and the w nodes

Concurrent writes — if two writes occur concurrently it is not clear which one happened first; the only safe solution is to merge the concurrent writes, and if a winner is picked based on a timestamp (last write wins), writes can be lost due to clock skew. A write concurrent with a read may be reflected on only some of the replicas, in which case it is undetermined whether the read returns the old or the new value

A partially failed write — if a write succeeded on some replicas but failed on others (for example because the disks on some nodes are full) and overall succeeded on fewer than w replicas, it is not rolled back on the replicas where it succeeded; so although the write was reported as failed, subsequent reads may or may not return the value from that write
If the coordinator crashes partway through a read, the client's automatic retry is guaranteed to reach a node holding the newest value for the key

questions.explanation: A retry guarantees nothing of the sort. The fourth genuine case is restoring from an old replica: if a node carrying a new value fails and is restored from one carrying an old value, the number of replicas holding the new value may fall below w. Six scenarios in all; note the deliberate hedge in the partially-failed-write case — 'may or may not'.

questions.question: What do quorum guarantees actually give you, and what don't they?

options.text: They adjust the probability of staleness rather than guaranteeing freshness
Quorums do guarantee strong consistency, in every configuration of w and r
Quorums automatically provide monotonic reads and read-your-writes as well
Quorums provide no guarantee of any kind, so w and r are merely advisory

questions.explanation: Note the word 'probability' — that is the honest description of what w and r buy you.

questions.question: How do you compute replication lag in a leader-based system, and what makes the computation possible?

options.text: Each node's position in the replication log, subtracted from the leader's
By comparing wall-clock timestamps reported by the leader and each follower
By counting the rows on each node and taking the difference between totals
It cannot be measured directly at all, only estimated from query latencies

questions.explanation: A single ordered log gives every node a scalar position, which is what makes subtraction meaningful. If a follower falls behind significantly the monitoring should alert you, which may indicate a problem in the network or an overloaded node.

questions.question: Why is monitoring staleness harder without a leader? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because in leaderless replication there is no fixed order in which writes are applied, so there is no single log position to compare
Because if the database only uses read repair with no anti-entropy process, there is no limit to how old a value might be — a value that is infrequently read may be ancient
Because leaderless databases maintain no version numbers for their stored values, so there is nothing to compare
Because a client cannot read from more than one replica per request, so it never sees the divergence at all

questions.explanation: There has been research on measuring replica staleness and predicting the expected percentage of stale reads depending on the parameters n, w and r — the chapter cites Bailis, Venkataraman, Franklin et al. on quantifying eventual consistency with PBS — but this is not yet common practice. The chapter's wish: eventual consistency is a deliberately vague guarantee, but for operability it's important to be able to quantify 'eventual'.

questions.question: Which benefits do properly configured quorums provide? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They let a database tolerate the failure of individual nodes without the need for failover
They tolerate individual nodes going slow, because requests don't have to wait for all n nodes to respond — they can return when w or r nodes have responded
They suit use cases that require high availability and low latency, and that can tolerate occasional stale reads
They guarantee that no stale value is ever returned to a client, under every possible failure scenario

questions.explanation: Failure and slowness tolerance without failover, for workloads that can accept occasional staleness.

questions.question: What fault motivates sloppy quorums, and what is odd about the nodes' status?

options.text: A network interruption can cut a client off from the nodes it needs
Every node has crashed simultaneously, so no quorum can possibly be formed
The disks on the home nodes are full, so all writes to them fail outright
The node clocks have drifted apart, so writes can no longer be ordered

questions.explanation: Alive but unreachable is the specific condition sloppy quorums address.

questions.question: Define sloppy quorum and hinted handoff.

options.text: Writes land on non-home nodes, later forwarded by hinted handoff
A sloppy quorum reduces w and r below the required threshold; hinted handoff retries failed writes
A sloppy quorum writes to fewer than w nodes; hinted handoff is a background repair
A sloppy quorum elects a temporary leader; hinted handoff demotes it

questions.explanation: The count is preserved; the membership of the set is relaxed.

questions.question: Why isn't a sloppy quorum a quorum at all?

options.text: It raises write availability but breaks the freshness guarantee
Because it contacts fewer than w nodes, so writes are not durable at all
Because it does not actually increase availability for writes in any way
Because it guarantees only freshness of reads, and never durability of writes

questions.explanation: Durability without overlap — the read set and write set may now be disjoint.

questions.question: Are sloppy quorums optional, and what are the defaults?

options.text: Optional everywhere: default on in Riak, off in Cassandra and Voldemort
They are mandatory in all three of Riak, Cassandra and Voldemort
They are enabled by default in all three of those implementations
They are disabled by default in all three of those implementations

questions.explanation: Riak differs from Cassandra and Voldemort on the default.

questions.question: How do Cassandra and Voldemort handle multi-datacenter operation?

options.text: n spans all datacenters, but the client waits only for a local quorum
They keep all communication local to one datacenter and replicate asynchronously between clusters
They require a quorum spanning all datacenters for every write
They elect a leader per datacenter

questions.explanation: Riak differs: it keeps all communication between clients and database nodes local to one datacenter, so n describes the number of replicas within one datacenter, and cross-datacenter replication between database clusters happens asynchronously in the background, similar to multi-leader replication. Leaderless replication suits multi-datacenter operation because it is designed to tolerate conflicting concurrent writes, network interruptions and latency spikes.

questions.question: Conflicts occur in Dynamo-style stores 'even if strict quorums are used'. On which additional occasions can they arise?

options.text: During read repair or hinted handoff
During compaction or snapshotting
During failover or leader election
Only when clients write concurrently; there are no other occasions

questions.explanation: Both are mechanisms that move values between nodes outside the normal write path, so both can introduce conflicts.

questions.question: Two clients concurrently write key X to a three-node store, and the nodes receive them in different orders. Trace the outcome node by node.

options.text: Three nodes receive two concurrent writes in different orders
All three nodes receive both writes in the same order, ending consistent
Node 1 receives both, nodes 2 and 3 receive neither
The writes are serialized by a coordinator, so no inconsistency arises

questions.explanation: Figure 5-12's caption: concurrent writes in a Dynamo-style datastore, where there is no well-defined ordering. Events may arrive in a different order at different nodes due to variable network delays and partial failures.

questions.question: How well do database implementations handle concurrent-write conflicts, and what does that oblige you to do?

options.text: Replicas must converge, but most implementations handle it poorly
All implementations handle conflicts correctly, so no work is needed
Conflict handling is entirely the database's responsibility
Conflicts cannot be avoided, so data loss is inevitable

questions.explanation: An unusually blunt transfer of responsibility to the application developer.

questions.question: Describe last write wins and the two products' stance on it.

options.text: Keep the write with the biggest timestamp and discard the rest
Merge all concurrent values; mandatory in Riak, optional in Cassandra
Pick the lowest timestamp; optional in both
Store all versions as siblings; mandatory in Cassandra

questions.explanation: Since neither client knew about the other one, it's not clear which happened first — it doesn't really make sense to say that either happened 'first': we say the writes are concurrent, so their order is undefined. The ordering LWW imposes is arbitrary.

questions.question: State the cost of LWW, including the claim most readers miss.

options.text: It converges, but silently discards concurrent writes that were acknowledged
It only ever discards writes that were genuinely concurrent with one another
It never discards a write at all; it merely reorders them by their timestamps
It costs nothing, because convergence comes free with timestamp comparison

questions.explanation: So LWW is not merely lossy for concurrent writes — clock skew can make it lose non-concurrent ones too.

questions.question: What is the only safe way to use a database with LWW?

options.text: Write each key only once and treat it as immutable, as with a UUID key
Synchronize every clock with NTP and rely on wall-clock timestamps instead
Apply last-write-wins to reads only, and resolve write conflicts in the app
Set w equal to n, so that every replica agrees before a write is accepted

questions.explanation: Write-once immutable keys make concurrency structurally impossible.

questions.question: Define the happens-before relationship and concurrency as the chapter does.

options.text: B happens after A if B knows about, depends on, or builds upon A
A happens before B if A's timestamp is smaller; concurrency means equal timestamps
A happens before B if A was sent from a lower-numbered node; concurrency means same node
A happens before B whenever A committed first, so true concurrency cannot arise

questions.explanation: Knowledge, not time, is the criterion — the chapter cites Lamport's Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System. Whether one operation happens before another is the key to defining what concurrency means.

questions.question: Of two operations where one increments a value the other inserted, and two where neither client knows of the other, which pair is concurrent?

options.text: Figure 5-9 is causal because B increments the value A inserted
Figure 5-9 is the concurrent one and Figure 5-12 is causally dependent
Both figures show concurrent operations with no causal link between them
Both figures show a clear causal dependency, so concurrency does not arise in either one

questions.explanation: Causal dependency in one, mutual ignorance in the other.

questions.question: The 'Concurrency, Time, and Relativity' box makes a counterintuitive claim. What is it?

options.text: No — concurrency means mutual unawareness, not overlap in time
That concurrency is defined purely by wall-clock overlap
That relativity makes concurrency impossible to define
That the speed of light sets the minimum replication lag

questions.explanation: Computer systems are more permissive about concurrency than physics, because the network can fail to deliver knowledge even when light had time to.

questions.question: In the shopping cart example, what does the server do when client 1 writes [milk, flour] carrying version number 1?

options.text: Version 1 supersedes [milk] but is concurrent with [eggs], so both are kept
It overwrites both [milk] and [eggs], leaving [milk, flour] as the only value
It rejects the write outright, because version 1 is already stale by then
It keeps all three of the values as siblings for the client to merge later

questions.explanation: The version number tells the server exactly which prior state the write is based on, so it can distinguish overwrites from concurrent values.
