If the shopping cart example strikes you as too inane, the chapter suggests imagining instead two air traffic controllers concurrently adding aircraft to the sector they are tracking.

questions.question: Plotting the shopping-cart operations as a graph of causal dependencies, what does it reveal?

options.text: Which operation happened before which — and that the client is never fully up to date, yet no writes are lost
It shows the physical network topology, proving all writes were serialized
It shows wall-clock timestamps, proving the writes were not concurrent
It shows that some writes are lost, which is unavoidable

questions.explanation: Never fully current, but never lossy — the two properties the algorithm buys.

questions.question: State the rules of the version-number algorithm. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The server maintains a version number for every key, increments it every time that key is written, and stores the new version number along with the value written
When a client reads a key, the server returns all values that have not been overwritten, as well as the latest version number. A client must read a key before writing

When a client writes a key it must include the version number from the prior read, and it must merge together all values that it received in the prior read (the response from a write request can be like a read, returning all current values, which allows chaining several writes)
On receiving a write, the server discards every earlier version of that key and retains only the newest value it has so far seen

questions.explanation: Discarding everything would destroy siblings. The genuine rule is that a write with a particular version number overwrites all values at that version or below, but must keep any higher-numbered values as siblings. Crucially, the server can determine whether two operations are concurrent by looking at the version numbers — it does not need to interpret the value itself, so the value could be any data structure. A write without a version number is concurrent with all other writes, so it will not overwrite anything and will just be returned as one of the values on subsequent reads.

questions.question: Riak calls concurrent values siblings. Merging [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] with [eggs, milk, ham], what is the result and what detail is worth noting?

options.text: The union gives [milk, flour, eggs, bacon, ham] with no duplicates
The merge yields [eggs, milk, ham] because it has the higher version
The merge duplicates milk and eggs, giving seven items
The siblings cannot be merged without losing data

questions.explanation: This is essentially the same problem as conflict resolution in multi-leader replication: you could pick one value based on a version number or timestamp (last write wins), but that implies losing data, so you may need to do something more intelligent in application code. The algorithm ensures that no data is silently dropped, at the cost of requiring clients to clean up afterward by merging the concurrently written values.

questions.question: Where does union merging break, and what is the fix called?

options.text: Removals reappear, so deletions need a tombstone marker instead
It breaks on additions; the fix is a version vector
It breaks on updates; the fix is last write wins
It does not break; union merging is always correct

questions.explanation: Merging siblings in application code is complex and error-prone, so Riak's CRDT datatype support can automatically merge siblings in sensible ways, including preserving deletions.

questions.question: Why is a single version number insufficient with multiple replicas, and what replaces it?

options.text: One version number per replica per key, collected into a version vector
A single version number is sufficient; version vectors are an optimization
Timestamps replace version numbers when there are multiple replicas
A global counter replaces the per-key version number

questions.explanation: Per-replica counters are what let a node distinguish 'I've seen this' from 'this is news to me'.

questions.question: Name the interesting version vector variant, the system using it, and Riak's name for the encoded form.

options.text: The dotted version vector, used in Riak 2.0 as a causal context string
The vector clock, used in Cassandra; Riak calls the encoding a digest
The Lamport timestamp, used in Voldemort; Riak calls it a hint
The hybrid logical clock, used in Riak 1.0; Riak calls it a tombstone

questions.explanation: Causal context travelling with the client is what makes cross-replica read-then-write safe.

questions.question: What cross-replica operation do version vectors make safe, and what is the caveat?

options.text: It is safe to read from one replica and write back to another
They make it safe to write to any replica with no siblings ever created
They make reads strongly consistent, with no caveat
They eliminate the need for application-level merging

questions.explanation: Safety here means no silent loss, not no work.

questions.question: The final box makes a terminology correction. What is it?

options.text: Also called a vector clock, though the two are not quite the same
Vector clocks and version vectors are identical terms
Vector clocks are the right structure for comparing replica state
Implementations use neither term, preferring to speak of causal context instead

questions.explanation: A commonly conflated pair, with a practical rule for which to reach for.

questions.question: Which purposes can replication serve? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High availability — keeping the system running even when one machine, or several machines, or an entire datacenter goes down
Disconnected operation — allowing an application to continue working when there is a network interruption
Latency — placing data geographically close to users, so that users can interact with it faster
Durability — guaranteeing that a write confirmed to the client can never be lost, even under asynchronous replication

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication explicitly cannot promise that. The fourth purpose the summary lists is scalability: handling a higher volume of reads than one machine could, by serving reads from replicas. Four purposes. Note that the scalability benefit is specifically about reads.
